topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; findings on digital competencies may have limited direct application to Australian organisational settings outside healthcare, though framework principles could inform broader AI literacy initiatives.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are prioritised in your region's public health or organisational frameworks — European models may differ from Australian standards, so benchmark against local capability requirements.

Use competency frameworks as a template to audit existing AI literacy gaps in your workforce; the scoping review likely identifies foundational versus advanced competencies that can guide targeted training design.

Consider how domain-specific competencies (e.g., for public health roles) can be adapted to your organisation's sector — the framework approach provides structure even if content differs from your context.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears focused on public health faculty development, but the specific geographic scope and institutional contexts are not indicated in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption is addressable through structured development programs; designing these programs to shift mindset from resistance to readiness is critical before rolling out AI literacy to students.
Public health educators need targeted professional development that covers both AI technical foundations and discipline-specific applications, rather than generic AI training.
Institutional support for faculty upskilling in AI should precede and underpin any broader AI literacy curriculum rollout in professional programs.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context. Applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development in Australia requires adaptation, as K-12 curriculum frameworks differ across countries.
takeaways: Consider scaffolding AI literacy into broader digital competency frameworks rather than teaching AI in isolation — this mirrors how effective workplace AI upskilling integrates with existing digital and domain skills.

Middle school AI curricula emphasize foundational concepts and hands-on practice; apply this principle to adult learners by combining conceptual grounding with practical exercises relevant to their role.

Holistic frameworks address ethics, critical thinking, and practical skills together — ensure your organization's AI literacy programs cover not just 'how to use AI tools' but also responsible use and critical evaluation.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education sector which may not directly translate to corporate workplace learning contexts. Generalisability depends on the specific strategies reviewed and their evidence base, which cannot be fully assessed from the title alone.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most relevant to your organisation's roles, then map existing higher education pedagogies (e.g. project-based learning, interdisciplinary teams) that could be adapted for employee upskilling programs.

Consider blended approaches combining technical AI literacy with domain-specific applications rather than generic 'AI awareness' training, as higher education models suggest contextualised learning improves retention and capability development.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — proposes a theoretical model for higher education contexts, but generalisability to other sectors (corporate, government) and geographic regions unclear without access to full article.
takeaways: Consider AI literacy as a foundational 'meta-skill' that integrates across multiple domains rather than a standalone technical competency — this framing may help position AI upskilling as central to broader capability development in your organisation.

A four-domain model suggests you should assess and develop AI literacy across distinct areas (likely technical, critical thinking, ethical, and organisational dimensions) — identify which domains your workforce needs most rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach.

The focus on 'academic management innovation' suggests frameworks developed in higher education settings may require adaptation for non-academic organisations — test whether this model fits your sector before rolling out.

articles.title: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on medical education curriculum design, which may not directly transfer to non-medical professional development contexts, though the competency-based framework approach could have broader application.
takeaways: Use a competency-based framework when designing AI literacy programs: define specific, measurable capabilities employees need rather than generic 'AI awareness' training.
Integrate assessment methods into your AI literacy curriculum from the start — don't treat evaluation as an afterthought; this helps ensure people actually develop the competencies you're targeting.

Consider domain-specific AI literacy needs for your sector (e.g. medical professionals need different AI competencies than general office workers); one-size-fits-all approaches are unlikely to be effective.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics not fully evident from the title and snippet alone. The 'double-edged' framing suggests nuanced findings applicable across sectors, but geographic scope and sample composition require review of the full article.
takeaways: AI adoption can have paradoxical effects on employee creativity — while automation may reduce routine cognitive load, it can also constrain divergent thinking if implementation narrows problem-solving autonomy. Design AI tools to augment rather than replace creative decision-making.

Organisations should monitor creativity outcomes during AI implementation, not just efficiency gains. Employee perception of whether AI supports or threatens their creative contribution influences adoption success and psychological safety around the technology.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to nursing populations and medical AI contexts; generalisability to other healthcare roles or non-clinical sectors unclear. Sample details not provided in snippet.
takeaways: Preserve and expand work autonomy as AI systems are introduced in healthcare settings; loss of autonomy may undermine wellbeing gains from AI readiness programs, even when staff are well-prepared for technology adoption.
Design AI implementation and training to enhance rather than constrain clinical decision-making — frame AI as a decision-support tool that augments nurse expertise rather than automates judgement.
Assess staff autonomy and psychological wellbeing alongside technical AI readiness metrics; readiness training alone is insufficient if implementation removes control over work processes.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — would depend on sample composition, industry sector, and geographic scope of the study, which are not indicated in the title or snippet provided.
takeaways: AI-enabled work systems can create both negative strain (e.g. job insecurity, cognitive overload) and positive resources (e.g. skill development, efficiency gains) simultaneously — managers should actively monitor and mitigate strain pathways while amplifying resource gains to protect employee wellbeing.

When implementing AI tools, assess which employee groups may experience net strain versus net resources; tailor support interventions (training, job redesign, psychological safety initiatives) to rebalance competing effects on wellbeing outcomes.
Track employee wellbeing metrics alongside AI adoption to identify whether strain or resource pathways are dominating in your context, allowing for real-time adjustment of implementation strategy.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings may be particularly relevant to organisational contexts with paternalistic leadership structures, which are more prevalent in certain cultural settings (e.g., East Asian organisations). Generalisability to egalitarian or distributed leadership models in Western organisations like Australia should be tested.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customisation and adaptation decisions — this increases their willingness to collaborate with AI rather than resist or underutilise it.

Under paternalistic leadership, creating space for 'AI crafting' (employees tailoring AI tools to their workflows) can bridge the gap between leader directives and genuine employee engagement with AI systems.

Design change management for AI adoption to address ownership and autonomy, not just technical training — employees who feel they have ownership over how AI is implemented show higher collaboration rates.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — likely limited to sample studied, but scope (sector, geography, sample size) cannot be determined from title and snippet provided.
takeaways: Clarify employee roles when introducing generative AI tools — role ambiguity appears to be a key barrier to effective human-AI collaboration, suggesting clear guidelines and job descriptions need updating.

Build self-efficacy through training and early wins — the dual-pathway finding implies that boosting confidence in using AI tools (alongside reducing role confusion) is critical for adoption and productive collaboration.

Consider both psychological barriers together — addressing role clarity alone may be insufficient if employees lack confidence; conversely, training without clarity about responsibilities may undermine adoption efforts.

articles.title: When humans and agents form a collective: a framework for collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When humans and agents form a collective: a framework for collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a conceptual framework rather than empirical findings. Applicability depends on how well the framework generalises across different organisational contexts, team structures, and AI system types.
takeaways: Use the collective intelligence framework to deliberately design human-AI team structures that clarify roles, decision boundaries, and knowledge-sharing protocols rather than assuming AI agents and humans will naturally collaborate effectively.

Assess your current AI-augmented teams against the framework's dimensions to identify gaps—such as insufficient feedback loops, unclear accountability, or misaligned incentives—that may be undermining collective performance.

When implementing persistent human-AI teams, prioritise building feedback mechanisms that allow humans and agents to learn from each other and adapt their working relationship over time, rather than treating the AI tool as static.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte report based on consulting experience across organisations, likely skewed toward large enterprises in developed economies; specific client contexts not disclosed, limiting direct applicability to smaller or non-corporate settings.
takeaways: Shift framing from 'AI adoption' (technology-first) to 'AI adaptation' (behaviour-first) to increase likelihood of sustained engagement and skill development among employees.

Design change interventions that explicitly target the human behaviours required for AI tools, not just the tools themselves — including how teams communicate, make decisions, and handle uncertainty with AI outputs.
Embed adaptation into organisational workflows and reward systems early, rather than treating behaviour change as a post-implementation add-on.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific case examples and implementation contexts may not directly transfer to all organisational settings or smaller enterprises.
takeaways: Structure AI transformation into distinct phases or 'horizons' to manage change expectations and resource allocation over time, rather than attempting all improvements simultaneously.
Link AI adoption to measurable business impact rather than treating implementation as an end goal — define specific performance outcomes you want to achieve at each transformation phase.
Use a phased approach to build organisational capability and momentum, allowing teams to learn and adapt practices before scaling to more complex AI applications.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone; appears to be a single empirical study. Generalisability depends on sample size, sector, and geographic scope not evident from title. Likely limited to the specific organisational context(s) studied.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger job crafting through two distinct pathways: stress-based (threat appraisal) and resource-based (opportunity appraisal), suggesting employees respond differently depending on how they interpret AI in their role.
Managers can influence job crafting outcomes by shaping how employees cognitively appraise AI — framing it as an opportunity rather than purely a threat may lead to more adaptive role adjustments.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a perspective piece from Stanford GSB without specified empirical research base, sample, or geographic scope. Findings may reflect US business school context and may not generalise to Australian workplaces or non-elite organisations.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption could reshape roles, then design targeted upskilling interventions before disruption occurs rather than reacting to it.

Use AI-driven workplace changes as a catalyst to clarify and communicate your organisation's values and mission, helping employees see how their evolving roles contribute to meaningful outcomes beyond efficiency gains.

articles.title: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited by lack of detail in snippet — geographic scope and sample characteristics unclear. Likely represents a single study with unknown sector and size constraints.
takeaways: Digital hoarding (excessive file/email retention) may stem from different psychological drivers (e.g., loss aversion, perfectionism, information overload anxiety) — understanding an individual's specific pathway helps target interventions more effectively than generic 'declutter' policies.

Workplace digital hoarding interventions should be personalised based on root cause rather than one-size-fits-all: loss-averse employees may need reassurance systems; overwhelmed employees may need better search/organisation tools.
Identifying distinct hoarding pathways can help managers address the behaviour without shame, potentially improving engagement with digital wellbeing and file management practices.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to full article, generalisability cannot be assessed. Likely depends on sample size, industry sectors studied, and geographic scope of organisations included.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger either approach behaviours (employees actively redesigning roles to leverage AI tools) or avoidance behaviours (resistance or withdrawal) — understanding which employees tend toward each response helps target support and change management strategies differently.

Job crafting during AI transitions is not passive acceptance but active employee agency — designing interventions that encourage approach-oriented crafting (e.g., skill-building, autonomy in tool adoption) may reduce avoidance and boost engagement.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven science reporting often oversimplifies neuroimaging findings; the actual study details, sample size, and methodology are not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies on psychopathy are prone to sensationalism; 'shocking differences' in neuroscience headlines often reflect small effect sizes or cherry-picked results rather than clear-cut biological divides.

Psychopathy exists on a spectrum and correlates with reduced empathic response in certain brain regions — but brain structure differences don't determine behaviour or moral culpability the way popular coverage often implies.

The gap between what neuroscience actually shows (localized activation patterns) and what people imagine ('psychopaths are wired differently') is a great reminder to dig into the methods before accepting the headline.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology details are not provided. Generalisability depends on how representative the wine review dataset is and whether findings hold across different cultural contexts and wine regions.
takeaways: Wine review language reveals personality patterns — an AI spotted links between how people describe wines and their personality traits, suggesting our everyday language choices leak clues about who we are.

This is a clever demonstration of AI's ability to spot hidden patterns in unstructured text data that humans might miss, showing how machine learning can extract psychological insights from mundane online behaviour.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet; appears to be laboratory-based research on personality and memory, which may not fully capture how surprise affects memory in real-world contexts.
takeaways: People don't all remember surprising moments the same way — your personality type shapes which unexpected events stick in your mind and which you forget.
This suggests why two people can witness the same shocking event yet remember completely different details: their individual personality traits act as a filter for what 'sticks' in memory.
The finding hints at why eyewitness accounts vary so much and why personality-driven differences in memory could explain some of the mysteries in how humans recall dramatic or unexpected moments.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the specific twin sample used; twin studies typically rely on volunteer samples and may not represent the full population diversity of political beliefs across different cultures or nations.
takeaways: Twin studies suggest authoritarian political beliefs have a measurable genetic component — counterintuitive because politics feels purely ideological, but nature and nurture both shape how we respond to authority.

The research hints that authoritarianism isn't simply learned from parents or absorbed from culture; inherited traits (possibly temperament, risk tolerance, or cognitive style) interact with environment to shape these worldviews.

Finding genetic roots in something as culturally variable as political ideology reveals how deeply biology influences what we assume are purely 'chosen' beliefs — a genuinely surprising window into the nature–nurture puzzle.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Findings suggest broad cross-cultural patterns in personality-music links, though specific musical genres and cultural contexts may vary by region.
takeaways: Your taste in music reveals something real about your personality — and this connection holds up across wildly different cultures, suggesting personality and music preference share universal roots.

People worldwide show consistent patterns: certain personality types gravitate toward similar musical styles, hinting that our musical choices tap into something deeper than just cultural conditioning.
A surprisingly direct window into what makes humans tick: music preference may be one of the easiest, most enjoyable ways to spot personality patterns in yourself and others.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — generalisability depends on study design, sample size, and cultural context, which are not detailed in the title or snippet provided.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism — traits like dominance, competitiveness, and low empathy — may paradoxically boost short-term romantic attraction, possibly because confidence and boldness read as attractive despite underlying selfishness.
The finding challenges the intuition that 'nice guys finish first' in romance, suggesting narcissistic charm can be initially seductive even when it signals poor partnership material long-term.
This reveals a mismatch between what attracts us immediately and what makes relationships work — a reminder that first impressions driven by charisma don't predict relationship quality.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not provided in snippet. The theoretical model linking AI adoption to depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership may apply across sectors, but actual applicability depends on study design, sample size, and geographic scope — further details needed from full article.
takeaways: AI adoption without strong ethical leadership and psychological safety may harm employee mental health — assess your organisation's ethical AI governance and leader capability before scaling adoption.

Psychological safety is a critical mediator of AI's impact on wellbeing; prioritise creating environments where employees feel safe raising concerns about AI systems, rather than treating adoption as purely technical.

Monitor for depression and mental health impacts during AI transitions, particularly among employees who lack voice or trust in how AI decisions are made — psychological safety interventions may be protective.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad but likely skewed toward developed economies and white-collar sectors typical of PwC's respondent base. Sample composition and methodology not detailed in snippet, limiting assessment of representativeness across geographies and industries.
takeaways: Use survey findings to benchmark your organisation's psychological safety climate against global peer perceptions—identify where workforce hopes and fears diverge from your current culture and prioritise interventions accordingly.

Consider which specific workforce concerns (e.g., job security, autonomy, trust in leadership) are most acute in your sector and design targeted safety interventions—generic approaches miss the mark when employee anxieties differ by role or geography.

articles.title: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Cannot be determined from title and snippet alone — insufficient information provided about study design, sample composition, geography, or methodology.
takeaways: Understanding how AI implementation affects employee emotional well-being is critical for psychological safety; organisations should monitor affective outcomes (stress, anxiety, engagement) during AI adoption to identify and address negative impacts early.

AI-driven changes to work can threaten psychological safety if employees fear job loss or feel depersonalised; proactive communication about AI's role and how human contributions remain valued can help maintain a safe, trusting workplace culture.

articles.title: Reframing workplace safety, wellbeing, and performance among operating room nurses in contemporary healthcare systems - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Reframing workplace safety, wellbeing, and performance among operating room nurses in contemporary healthcare systems  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on operating room nurses in healthcare settings; findings may not generalise to other high-stress professions or non-clinical workplaces, and geographic scope is unclear from the snippet.
takeaways: Psychological safety in high-stakes environments like operating rooms requires explicit reframing of how safety, wellbeing, and performance are connected — treating them as interdependent rather than competing priorities.

Healthcare leaders should assess whether current safety protocols inadvertently undermine psychological safety by creating fear-based reporting cultures; consider how to shift from blame to learning-oriented approaches.

OR teams may benefit from structured practices that normalise speaking up about concerns and mistakes, as psychological safety directly affects both individual wellbeing and team performance outcomes.

articles.title: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams - Deloitte
articles.snippet: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Deloitte briefing based on proprietary research or consulting experience; specific sample size, methodology, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Prioritise capability development alongside team composition when designing for high performance — this reframes recruitment and hiring decisions to include assessment of developmental potential, not just current skills.

Map psychological safety explicitly to human capability development; teams where members feel safe to admit gaps and ask for help are more likely to close capability gaps through peer learning and mentorship.

articles.title: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — appears to synthesise existing research on AI workplace impacts, but without clarity on geographic or sectoral scope, applicability to specific Australian organisational contexts may vary.
takeaways: Implement co-skilling programmes (training employees in AI alongside their existing roles) to reduce job insecurity and build psychological safety around technological change.
Provide visible organisational support through transparent communication about AI implementation, career pathways, and job security commitments—this directly buffers against anxiety and builds trust.
Address job insecurity proactively as a psychological safety issue; employees who fear redundancy are less likely to experiment with new tools, ask questions, or voice concerns about AI integration.
